title: Oncall-first trace-handoff reporter and SLO-alerting wiring for Tempo
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Problem: When SLO alerts fire (latency or error-rate violations) on customer routes we do not have an automated, oncall-friendly way to capture a representative set of spans and hand them off to Tempo with context. This slows incident TTR because engineers must manually reconstruct traces, find tenant/time windows, and stitch artifacts across logs and metrics.

Goals:
- Provide an automated 'trace-handoff reporter' that triggers when a configured SLO alert occurs and:
  1) captures a bounded snapshot of high-cardinality spans (root->N depth) for affected tenants and routes,
  2) enriches spans with alert context (alert id, timeframe, probe metadata, relevant console runbook link),
  3) writes the snapshot to Tempo/trace storage using a lightweight signed envelope that supports short-term retention and quick retrieval, and
  4) surfaces a one-click link in the alert/incident that opens a pre-filtered trace view in Console.
- Keep per-tenant privacy and quota controls (do not exceed tenant write budgets).
- Fail gracefully: if Tempo write fails, place snapshot in durable backfill queue and annotate the incident with backfill id.

Non-goals:
- Full raw-span re-ingest for long-term archival (handled by long-term pipeline).
- Replacing existing OTLP ingestion paths for customer traffic; this is a targeted incident capture flow.

Design summary:
- Trigger points: alerting rules in Console (latency_p99, error_rate_windowed) will call the new Handoff API on the observability control plane.
- Handoff API collects span IDs via a lightweight sampler running in the sampling pipeline (hooked into the ingest path) that can assemble span trees for a tenant/time window up to 10k spans or 2MB payload.
- Snapshot assembly uses deterministic sampling heuristics: prioritize errored spans, high-latency spans, and spans touching public-facing routes.
- Envelope: each snapshot is packaged as a signed, compressed envelope (AES-GCM for payload encryption, HMAC for integrity) with metadata headers (alert_id, tenant_id, window_start, window_end, retention_ttl).
- Write: attempt direct write to Tempo ingest endpoint via a tenant-scoped write token. On transient failures, push envelope to the durable backfill queue (see dependency ENG-271001).
- Retrieval UX: Console will accept the envelope id in alert context and decode/display a pre-filtered trace timeline and quick links to related logs/metrics.

Trade-offs and rationale:
- Why envelopes vs direct span write? Envelopes let us attach alert metadata and defer expensive rehydration if Tempo is overloaded; they also make backfill retries idempotent.
- Why limited snapshot size? To bound cost and avoid overloading Tempo during incidents. We choose a conservative default (10k spans / 2MB) and provide tenant overrides for enterprise customers.
- Security: envelopes are encrypted; writes require tenant write tokens. We avoid adding broad new permissions to the ingest plane.

Success criteria (measurable):
- TTR reduction: median time to first relevant trace in incidents for targeted SLO alerts improves by >= 40% for cases where traces previously needed manual lookup.
- Reliability: snapshot write success >= 99% over 30 days; backfill fallback recorded and retried for failures.
- Cost: average snapshot size < 1MB and per-incident storage cost under budget (tracked by new cost metric).

Rollout plan:
- Phase 1 (canary, 2 weeks): internal tenants only. Instrument alert firing path to create no-op handoff events and validate telemetry.
- Phase 2 (beta, 4 weeks): opt-in for 10 customers; monitor write success, backfill queue latency, and oncall usage.
- Phase 3 (GA): enable by default with tenant quotas; expose console settings to control capture thresholds and retention TTL.

Monitoring and dashboards:
- New Console dashboard: Handoff success rate, average snapshot size, time-to-first-trace link click in incidents, backfill queue depth, Tempo write latency per-region.
- Alerts: Handoff failure rate > 1% for 10m (P1), backfill queue depth > threshold (P2).

Testing plan:
- Unit tests for envelope packaging/unpacking and HMAC verification.
- Integration test: simulated alert triggers generate envelope -> Tempo write (mock) -> console link resolves to decoded view.
- E2E: load test 100 concurrent incidents, each producing a 2MB snapshot, verify queueing and backfill behavior.

Open decisions:
- TTL default: 7 days vs 14 days (cost vs post-incident forensic window). Current default set to 7 days; product to confirm.
- Sampling knobs exposure to tenants: expose coarse controls (high/medium/low) in GA; expose numeric limits only for enterprise.

Related artifacts:
- Design doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/OBS/Trace+Handoff+Reporter+Design (draft)
- Initial prototype PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra/pull/7051 (prototype hooks)
- Oncall playbook draft in Drive: https://drive.redwood.ai/drive/folders/1OncallTraceHandoff (internal)

Playbook excerpt for oncall:
- When SLO alert fires and the alert shows a Handoff Link -> click link to open pre-filtered trace view. If link shows 'BACKFILL_PENDING', escalate to infra oncall and reference backfill id.
- If alert lacked a Handoff Link but the incident is high-sev, run the handoff diagnostic script (link in playbook) to trigger a manual snapshot and attach envelope to incident.

Notes on privacy and compliance:
- Snapshots exclude raw PII fields by default via the same attribute sanitizer used in the main ingest pipeline. High-trust enterprise customers may opt-in to include additional fields under a contract.

Next steps:
- Finish prototype envelope format and write a full integration test with a tempo mock.
- Product confirm TTL and tenant-facing controls by 2026-02-20.
- Schedule canary for internal tenants starting 2026-03-01.
